title: AdaBoost
text:
AdaBoost, short for adaptive boosting, is a supervised method that combines many weak models into one strong one. It belongs to the family of ensemble methods, which combine the predictions of many models instead of relying on one. There are two main ways to build an ensemble of trees (first figure below). In bagging, which random forests use, each tree is trained on its own random resample of the training data, independently of the others, so all the trees could be trained at the same time, and the final prediction is a majority vote in which every tree counts once. In boosting, the models are built one after another, and each new model concentrates on the examples that the earlier ones got wrong. The order matters, because each model depends on the results of the one before. Bagging mainly steadies deep trees whose answers change a lot from one sample to the next, while boosting mainly strengthens very simple models that on their own miss too much. AdaBoost is used for tasks such as detecting faces in images, flagging fraudulent transactions and scoring customers, and it led to the gradient boosting methods on the later pages of this site.
AdaBoost usually boosts decision stumps. A stump is a decision tree with a single question, a root and two leaves, such as “Is the department Forward Deployed Engineering?”. On its own a stump is a weak model, only a little better than guessing, but hundreds of stumps, each concentrating on a different part of the data, can add up to a strong one. Because each stump asks about one feature, the combined model is still possible to inspect: the features its stumps ask about most are the ones it relies on.
Every training row starts with the same weight. In each round, AdaBoost fits a stump to the weighted rows, choosing the question with the lowest weighted error ε, the total weight of the rows the stump gets wrong. It then raises the weight of the rows the stump got wrong, lowers the weight of the rows it got right, and rescales the weights so that they add up to 1. The next stump is fitted to these new weights, so it pays most attention to the rows that earlier stumps found hard.
Each stump also gets a weight of its own, its say in the final vote, written α (alpha). In the classic two-class version, α = ½ ln((1 − ε) / ε). A stump that is right on most of the weighted rows has a small error and a large α, while a stump that does no better than a coin toss, with ε = 0.5, gets α = 0 and no say at all. The same α sets how much the row weights change: the weight of a row the stump got wrong is multiplied by exp(α), and the weight of a row it got right by exp(−α). The scikit-learn version used here, called SAMME, works the same way for more than two classes. It uses α = ln((1 − ε) / ε) + ln(K − 1), where K is the number of classes, so a stump only has to beat random guessing among the three role families, and it multiplies only the weights of the wrong rows, by exp(α), before rescaling, which has the same effect. A learning rate shrinks every α by the same factor. With a smaller learning rate each stump counts for less, so more rounds are needed, but the result is often more stable.
To label a new example, every stump votes for the class it predicts, with a vote worth its α, and the class with the largest total wins. With two classes this is the sign of α1·h1 + α2·h2 + …, where each stump’s vote h is +1 or −1.
A small example shows how this works (second figure below). Ten made-up points lie on a line at x = 0 to 9, with classes + + + − − − + + + −. No single cut point separates the two classes. Every point starts with a weight of 0.1.

The final vote, weighted by each stump’s α, puts all ten points in the right class, although no single stump does.

title: AdaBoost
text:
Data Preparation
AdaBoost is supervised, so like the decision trees it can only learn from labelled data. Every posting needs its role family attached, because each stump learns which answer to its question goes with which role, and a posting without a label gives it nothing to learn from and nothing to check against. The labels and the 1,159 postings are the same as on the Decision Trees page: 721 software_eng, 275 solutions and 163 forward_deployed. The job title, the seniority level and the flag for repeated copies are never used as features, because the label is read from the title.
AdaBoost also uses the same split, so its results can be compared with tree 1 posting by posting. The postings were divided at random into a training set of 927 (80%) and a test set of 232 (20%), stratified so that each role family has the same share in both. The two sets are disjoint, meaning no posting is in both, and this was checked by job ID. The stumps, the number of rounds and the learning rate are all chosen using the training set only, and the test set is used once, at the end, to measure how well the model labels postings it has never seen. If test postings were also in the training set, the model would be graded on examples it had already seen, and its accuracy would look better than it really is.
AdaBoost in scikit-learn, like the decision trees it is built from, only accepts numbers. The features are the nine used by tree 1: four categories, which are the department, the company, the location and the working arrangement, and five numbers, which are the bottom and top of the yearly salary range, the length of the description in characters, the number of locations listed and whether more than one location is listed. The four category columns were one-hot encoded: each category becomes its own column, which is 1 for postings in that category and 0 for all others (first table below). The working arrangement, for example, becomes four columns, for hybrid, onsite, remote and missing, and each posting has a 1 in exactly one of them. A missing category was given its own value, “missing”, before encoding. A missing number was filled with the median of the training set, and an extra 0/1 column marks postings with no salary. The salary is the one from the job board’s salary field, as for tree 1, not the pay ranges read from the description text on the Regression page, so that the two models see exactly the same data. After encoding, the nine columns become 222. The encoder and the medians were learned from the training set alone and applied unchanged to the test set, and a category that appears only in test postings becomes a row of zeros.


One-hot encoding: ten of the 1,159 postings, with the working arrangement and the company beside the 0/1 columns they become. Each posting has a 1 in the column for its own category and 0 in the others. All four working-arrangement columns are shown, but only 6 of the 19 company columns, the ones these ten postings use. Job IDs are shortened in this image, and the linked file has them in full. The same ten postings, in the same order, appear before encoding, with all nine of tree 1’s features, in the first table on the Decision Trees page.



Training set: ten of the 927 training postings as the stumps receive them, after encoding and filling in missing values. The table shows the five number columns, the 0/1 column for a missing salary and 4 of the 216 one-hot columns, the four that are 1 for the most training postings. Eight of these ten postings have no salary, so their salary columns hold the training medians, $226,000 and $380,000.



Test set: ten of the 232 test postings, encoded with the categories and medians learned from the training set. None of their job IDs is in the training set, and their labels are only used to score the predictions.

Data files

Raw data: job postings collected from company job boards with the Apify multi-ATS job scraper, using fetch_apify.py. The full raw files are about 64 MB and are not stored in the repository, so a 20-row raw sample is linked instead.
Clean data: ats_final.csv, the 4,294 cleaned postings this page starts from, before repeated copies are removed and the three role families are selected.
Input sample before encoding: dt_input_sample.csv, the same ten postings with their role family and the nine features before the categories are encoded and missing values filled, shown in the first table on the Decision Trees page.

title: AdaBoost
text:
Results
AdaBoost was tuned on the training postings only. Its two settings, the number of rounds (n_estimators) and the learning rate, depend on each other, so they were tuned together by 5-fold cross-validation over every pair of learning rate 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1 and 1.5 with 10, 25, 50, 100, 200, 300, 500, 750, 1,000 and 1,500 rounds. The training postings were split into five parts, and each part was held out in turn while AdaBoost learned from the other four. Each fold’s model was grown once to 1,500 rounds and scored after every round, which gives the validation accuracy at every number of rounds (figure 1). The best pair was learning rate 1 with 750 rounds, with a cross-validated accuracy of 0.894; when two pairs scored the same, the one with fewer rounds would have been kept. That model was then fitted on all 927 training postings and scored once on the 232 test postings. As on the earlier pages, always guessing software_eng would be right for 62.1% of test postings, so that is the level any model has to beat. Like tree 1, it relies mostly on department, which makes up 77.8% of its feature importance, far ahead of company (9.2%) and location (7.6%). title: AdaBoost
text:
Conclusions
Combining hundreds of very simple questions did not sort job postings better than one more detailed set of questions. Asking about one fact at a time, such as which team a job belongs to or which city it is in, with each new question aimed at the postings the earlier ones got wrong, sorted about 87 in every 100 new postings correctly. The single decision tree from the previous page, built on the same facts, sorted about 92 in every 100.
Nearly all of the difference came from solutions jobs. The combined questions often mistook solutions jobs for software engineering, while the single tree, which can follow one question with another about the same posting, told them apart more often. Both relied most on the name of the team the employer gives the job, which shows again that the way employers organise their hiring carries much of what can be told about a job.
On the wording of the job descriptions, the same approach did better than a single tree and as well as the methods of the Naive Bayes page, getting about 92 in every 100 right. The words of a posting remain the clearest sign of what kind of job it is.
For the question of how AI is changing tech hiring, the new forward deployed role is easiest to recognise from what the job asks people to do. Facts such as the team, the place and the pay mostly reflect the employer, and more elaborate ways of combining those facts do not reveal more about the jobs themselves.

title: Introduction
text:
On September 4, 2026, software development job postings on Indeed stood about 24 percent below their level in February 2020. In early 2022, the same postings had been more than twice as high as in February 2020 (Indeed, via FRED). That rise and fall raises a simple question: what slowed tech hiring down? Three explanations compete: higher interest rates, new AI tools that can do some of the work, and a reset after tech companies hired too many people during the pandemic. Signs of all three appeared in 2022. In March 2022, the Federal Reserve began raising interest rates from near zero. By July 2023, its main rate had reached 5.25 to 5.5 percent (Federal Reserve, 2022; 2023). In late November 2022, OpenAI released ChatGPT. About two months later, it had 100 million users a month, a pace faster than TikTok or Instagram (TIME). In the same month as ChatGPT’s release, Meta let go of more than 11,000 employees (Meta). The slowdown also reached the wider economy. Job openings across the United States peaked at about 12.3 million in March 2022, a figure first reported as 11.5 million (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, May 2022) and later revised up. By July 2026, that number had fallen to 7.3 million (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics).



Monthly job openings in the United States, 2015 to 2026. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.


The answer matters because each explanation points to a different future. If higher interest rates caused the slowdown, hiring could pick up again as borrowing gets cheaper. If AI tools now do work that people used to do, some of those jobs may not return. If companies simply hired too many people during the pandemic, the drop may be a one-time reset. Meta’s cut in November 2022 came to about 13 percent of its staff. Its chief executive, Mark Zuckerberg, wrote that online shopping had returned to its earlier trends after the pandemic (Meta). More than 191,000 workers at U.S. tech companies lost their jobs in 2023 alone (Crunchbase News). People at the start of their careers may face the hardest path. In early 2026, only 4.5 percent of software development job postings on Indeed were for entry-level roles, while 69.3 percent were for senior roles (Indeed Hiring Lab). Between November 2022 and June 2026, employment of workers aged 22 to 25 fell about 11 percent in the jobs most open to AI. Over the same period, employment of workers the same age in jobs less open to AI grew about 10 percent. That leaves young workers in the jobs most open to AI about 19 percent behind their peers (Stanford update, August 2026). Students choosing a subject, colleges planning courses and employers planning teams all need to know which explanation fits.
Researchers have already started to study this question. Their early findings point in different directions. In August 2025, Stanford researchers reported a 13 percent drop in employment for workers aged 22 to 25 in the jobs most open to AI. They measured that drop against young workers in jobs less open to AI. The figure also takes account of wider hiring changes at the same companies (Stanford working paper, August 2025). The 19 percent gap in the August 2026 update comes from a simpler comparison that leaves those company changes out. The same update found no widespread job losses across the economy linked to AI (Stanford update, August 2026). With that text left in, postings grouped by employer rather than by kind of job, and 12 of the 14 groups each held postings from a single company. text:
Research Questions

How much did tech job postings rise and fall between 2019 and 2026, and how does that compare with other kinds of jobs?
Did tech job postings start to fall before or after ChatGPT was released in late November 2022?
How closely does the fall in tech job postings line up with the interest rate rises that began in March 2022?
Do government counts of job openings, hires and quits tell the same story as online job postings?
Has the number of people working in software and data jobs kept growing, even as job postings fell?
What kinds of roles do AI companies post most often, and how many of them are customer-facing technical roles?
How many openings at AI companies are for entry-level workers compared with senior workers?
How much pay do AI companies advertise for different kinds of roles?

curl "https://hacker-news.firebaseio.com/v0/item/18807017.json"

curl -X POST "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/scrapesage~multi-ats-job-scraper/run-sync-get-dataset-items" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $APIFY_TOKEN" \

Six daily rows of the Indeed posting index for Software Development in the United States, where the index is set to 100 on 1 February 2020 and is not a count of postings.

Six monthly observations of one JOLTS series as the API returns them, with the year, the period code and the period name in separate fields and the series identified only by its code.

Six rows for one occupation as they appear in the annual OEWS workbooks, one file per year, where the year itself is recoverable only from the file name.

Every source went through the same seven cleaning steps in the same order. The steps were loading and deduplication, text and field cleaning, field extraction, missing values, normalisation, outliers, and discretisation. Not every step applied to every source. The Indeed, BLS and OEWS files arrived as tidy tables of numbers, so they had no text to clean and no fields to pull out. Only the Hacker News and job board data were sorted into bands, such as short, medium and long posts. Rows were removed for only two cleaning reasons. The job board exports held 115 repeat copies of the same jobs, identical except for the time they were collected. Only the newest copy of each was kept. Hacker News had 3,744 comments marked as deleted or dead, and almost all of them were too short to hold a real job post. The OEWS files were also cut down to the six occupations the project follows. Every other row stayed in. Rows that looked wrong, unusual or repeated were marked with a flag. That way, each analysis can decide for itself what to leave out.
Some values are still missing on purpose. Of the 4,294 job board postings, 2,773 list no salary. All 2,244 postings from companies that use Greenhouse are in that group, because Greenhouse has no salary field at all. The other 529 are Ashby and Lever postings that left pay out. Filling these gaps with a guess would invent pay that was never offered, so they were left empty and marked with a flag. City names were read from the job board location text, which raised city coverage from 35 to 92 percent. Some Hacker News posts gave no work arrangement in their first line. For those, the rest of the text was searched, which raised coverage from 39 to 91 percent. Values found this way are marked, so they can be told apart from values in the first line.
Outliers were checked with a different method for each source, because each source holds a different kind of data. In the BLS and Indeed series, a value was flagged when it sat far outside the normal range of its own series. Salaries were checked against a fixed range of $20,000 to $1,000,000 a year. OEWS flagged any change of more than 20 percent from one year to the next. Most flags in the series turned out to be real events. Across all nonfarm jobs in the US, BLS counted about 13 million layoffs and discharges in March 2020, when COVID closed much of the economy. Nine of the 12 BLS flags fall between March and June 2020. More than 90 percent of the Indeed sector, state and metro flags fall between March 2020 and December 2021. These COVID-era values were kept in the data, because they record real events. Most of the 12 salary flags look like pay entered in the wrong unit, such as a Talent Coordinator role listed at $32 a year.
A review of how labels changed also turned up a real problem in the rules. Seniority was read from each job title with a list of keyword rules. When a title matched more than one rule, the later rule won. The intern rule looked for the letters “intern” anywhere in a title. That meant it also matched words such as “International” and “Internal”. In most of those titles, a later rule for manager or senior roles replaced the wrong label, which hid the mistake. The problem only showed up after a separate fix stopped later rules from replacing intern and new graduate labels. That fix was meant to stop “Associate Product Manager, New Grad” from being labelled as a lead role. Instead, 23 titles such as “International Tax Manager” were suddenly labelled as internships. The intern rule was changed to match only the whole word. That change also corrected 7 titles, such as “Software Engineer, International”, that had been wrong from the start. A similar check found that the rule for the abbreviation “Sr” matched the letters inside “Israel” and “SRE”. That rule was fixed the same way.

text:
Exploratory Data Visualizations



  
    
  
  
    1. Job postings index: AI-exposed against control sectors
    Between their March 2022 peak and August 2026, job postings in AI-exposed sectors fell roughly 67% and remain below their pre-pandemic level, while control sectors fell roughly 36% and recovered above theirs. The divergence begins several months before the ChatGPT release, indicating that AI cannot be the sole cause and that interest rate increases and the correction of pandemic-era overhiring also contributed.
  



  
    
  
  
    2. Job openings against online postings
    Job openings in the information sector and online postings in AI-exposed sectors both peak in spring 2022 and decline afterwards, confirming the trend in official government data as well as in commercial posting indices. Openings fall roughly 63% from peak while postings fall roughly 67%. The two falls are similar in size, so the online postings and the official count of vacancies tell the same story.
  



  
    
  
  
    3. Hires and quits in the information sector
    Hires in the information sector averaged 80,000 to 95,000 monthly through 2015 to 2019, peaked at 125,000 in 2021, and returned to roughly 75,000 by 2026 — close to the pre-pandemic range. Quits fell further, to 28,000 by 2026 against a 40,000 to 48,000 baseline, indicating a market where both employers and workers became less active rather than one where hiring simply collapsed.
  



  
    
  
  
    4. Employment by computer occupation
    Employment in software development rose from 1.36 million in 2021 to 1.69 million in 2025, and data science employment grew from 105,000 to 261,000 over the same period. Employment therefore expanded while job postings fell sharply, indicating that reduced advertising did not correspond to reduced headcount in these occupations.
  



  
    
  
  
    5. Role families across company job postings
    Engineering roles account for 839 of 4,294 postings, while customer-facing technical roles — forward deployed and solutions combined — account for 572, close to two-thirds of the engineering total. The 245 forward deployed postings confirm the role exists at scale rather than being a label used by one or two firms.
  



  
    
  
  
    6. Forward deployed and solutions postings by company
    Databricks and Palantir account for 178 of 245 forward deployed postings, or 73% of the total, while the remaining ten companies contribute 67 between them. The ratio of forward deployed to solutions roles also differs sharply by company — Palantir posts more than twice as many forward deployed as solutions, while Databricks, Asana and Ramp show the reverse — suggesting the two titles are used interchangeably by some employers and distinctly by others.
  



  
    
  
  
    7. Seniority mix within each role family
    Solutions roles are 53% staff level while forward deployed roles are only 4% staff, concentrating instead at mid (43%) and senior (29%). The two titles therefore differ in seniority profile as well as in name, which weakens the reading that they are interchangeable labels for the same work.
  



  
    
  
  
    8. Advertised salary by role family
    Research roles show the highest median advertised minimum at roughly $380,000, followed by software engineering, data and applied AI in a band around $220,000 to $230,000, while recruiting sits lowest at about $130,000. The unusually narrow forward deployed distribution reflects a single employer posting one standard band across its engineering roles rather than a genuine market pattern.
  



  
    
  
  
    9. Description length and advertised salary
    Description length shows no relationship with advertised salary across 1,459 postings, with a correlation of 0.00 and a flat fitted line. Combined with the near-identical length distributions across role families, this indicates description length reflects employer writing conventions rather than the seniority, complexity or compensation of the role.
  



  
    
  
  
    10. Work arrangement over time
    Remote postings rose from 30% of those stating a work arrangement in 2019 to a peak of 82% in 2022, then fell to 55% by 2026, while hybrid arrangements grew from almost nothing to 17% over the same period. The partial reversal suggests employers consolidated around hybrid rather than returning fully to onsite work.
  



  
    
  
  
    11. Most common locations in job postings
    Remote appears in 8,112 postings, more than any single city and 29% above San Francisco at 6,297, while five Bay Area locations together account for 6,657. Postings concentrate heavily in a handful of established technology hubs, with the top three locations covering more than the remaining seventeen combined.

title: Decision Trees
text:
A decision tree is a supervised method that predicts a class, or a number, by asking a series of yes-or-no questions about the features of an example. Each question sits at a node, such as “Is the job in San Francisco?” or “Is the top of the salary range at most $316,500?”. Each answer leads down a branch to the next question, until a leaf is reached. The leaf gives the prediction, which is the most common class among the training examples that ended up there. Trees are easy to read and explain, work with numeric and categorical features, need no scaling of the data, and pick up on combinations of features without being told about them. They are used for tasks such as credit scoring, medical triage and predicting which customers will leave, and they are the building block of methods that combine many trees, such as random forests and the boosting methods on the later pages of this site.
A tree is grown from the top down. All training examples start together at the root. The algorithm tries every feature and every possible cut point, and picks the question that splits the examples into the two purest groups, meaning groups that are each mostly one class. It then repeats this on each of the two groups, and so on, until the groups are pure or a stopping rule is reached, such as a maximum depth. The search is greedy: at each node it takes the best split available there, without looking ahead to the splits that could follow.
Gini impurity and entropy are the two usual ways to measure how mixed a group is. Gini impurity is one minus the sum of the squared class shares, which is the chance that two examples drawn at random from the group belong to different classes. Entropy is minus the sum of each class share times its base-2 logarithm, measured in bits. Both are 0 for a pure group and largest when the classes are evenly mixed: with two classes, Gini reaches 0.5 and entropy 1 bit (first figure below). To judge a split, the impurity of the two child groups is averaged, weighting each child by its size, and subtracted from the impurity of the parent. With entropy this decrease is called information gain, and the split with the largest gain is chosen. Gini and entropy almost always rank splits the same way. Gini is a little faster because it needs no logarithms, while entropy has a meaning in information theory, as the number of bits needed to describe the class.
A small example shows how this works (second figure below). A group of 100 examples holds 50 of class A and 50 of class B. A split sends 40 examples, all class A, to the left and 60 examples, 10 of class A and 50 of class B, to the right.

It is generally possible to create an infinite number of trees from the same data. For a numeric feature such as salary, any cut point between two neighbouring values divides the training examples in the same way, so there are infinitely many cut points to choose from, and each one gives a different tree for new examples that fall in between. On top of that, every node can ask about any feature, the tree can stop at any depth, and settings such as the smallest allowed leaf and the measure of impurity can all change. Even a small change in the training examples can change the question at the root, and with it every question below. The number of possible trees is therefore unlimited. The algorithm does not search all of them. It grows one tree greedily, and settings such as the maximum depth are chosen by testing them, as is done in this project.
This project uses decision trees to predict the same three role families as the Naive Bayes page: forward deployed engineering, solutions roles and software engineering. Three of the trees work from structured facts about each posting: its department, company, location, working arrangement, salary range, length of description and number of locations. Trees show which of these facts separate the roles, and the order of the questions shows which facts matter most. A fourth tree reads the same description words as the Naive Bayes models, so the two methods can be compared directly.

title: Decision Trees
text:
Data Preparation
Decision trees are supervised, so like Naive Bayes they can only learn from labelled data. Every posting needs its role family attached, because the tree learns which answers to its questions go with which role, and a posting without a label gives it nothing to learn from and nothing to check against. The labels are the same as on the Naive Bayes page, taken from each posting’s job title by keyword rules. The title itself is never used as a feature, and neither are two other columns built from it: the seniority level, which is read from the title by the same kind of rule, and the flag for repeated copies, which is matched on the title. Any of these would let the tree find the answer it is meant to predict.
The data is the same 1,159 postings as on the Naive Bayes page: 721 software_eng, 275 solutions and 163 forward_deployed. It also uses the same split, so the results of the two methods can be compared. The postings were divided at random into a training set of 927 (80%) and a test set of 232 (20%), stratified so that each role family has the same share in both. The two sets are disjoint, meaning no posting is in both, and this was checked by job ID. A tree is grown on the training set only, and the test set is used once, at the end, to measure how well it labels postings it has never seen. If test postings were also in the training set, the tree would be graded on examples it had already memorised, and its accuracy would look better than it really is.
Each posting is described by nine features. Four are categories: the department, which is the team name the employer gives on its job board; the company; the location; and the working arrangement, which is onsite, hybrid or remote. Five are numbers: the bottom and top of the yearly salary range, the length of the description in characters, the number of locations listed, and whether more than one location is listed. Some of these are often missing. The working arrangement is missing for 62% of postings and the salary range for 69%. A missing category was given its own value, “missing”. A missing number was filled with the median of the training set, and an extra yes-or-no column marks postings with no salary, so the tree can still use the fact that a company did not publish one. Four salaries that were clearly wrong were treated as missing, and 11 salaries given in British pounds were kept as stated.
Decision trees in scikit-learn, the Python library used here, only accept numbers. The four category columns were therefore one-hot encoded: each category becomes its own column, which is 1 for postings in that category and 0 for all others. For example, the column “location_clean = San Francisco, CA” is 1 for San Francisco postings. The questions in the tree diagrams below read “location_clean = San Francisco, CA <= 0.5”, which is true for postings outside San Francisco. The encoder and the medians were learned from the training set alone and then applied to the test set. Categories that appear only in test postings, such as the departments of 16 test postings and the locations of 7, become a row of zeros. Trees do not need the numbers to be scaled, because each question only compares one value with a cut point.
Four trees were built, each from a different set of features. Tree 1 uses all nine features, which become 222 columns after encoding. Early results showed that department alone separates the role families very well, because many employers name their teams after the role, such as “Field Engineering” or “Forward Deployed Engineering”. So tree 2 leaves out department (115 columns), and tree 3 also leaves out company (96 columns), to see how much the remaining facts about a posting can tell. Tree 4 ignores these features and uses only the description text, with company boilerplate removed and role phrases masked, turned into the same 3,631 TF-IDF word columns as on the Naive Bayes page.


Labelled input: ten of the 1,159 postings, each with its role family label and the nine features, before the categories are encoded and missing values filled. NaN marks a missing value. The departments show how varied the employers’ team names are, from “Field Engineering - Other” at Databricks to “Delta” at Palantir. Job IDs are shortened in this image, and the linked file has them in full.



Training set: ten of the 927 training postings. The tree, the category columns and the medians used to fill missing values are all learned from rows like these.



Test set: ten of the 232 test postings. None of their job IDs is in the training set. They are encoded with the categories learned from the training set, and their labels are only used to score the tree’s predictions.

The gap is training accuracy minus test accuracy. A large gap means the tree has learned details of the training postings that do not carry over to new ones, which is known as overfitting. Macro F1 is the average F1 score of the three classes, as on the Naive Bayes page, so the small forward_deployed class counts as much as the large software_eng class.

Choosing the depth
Deeper trees fit the training postings more closely, but past some depth they stop doing better on the postings held out during cross-validation (figure 1). For tree 1, cross-validation accuracy keeps rising until the depth is unlimited (0.891), so its Gini tree grows until every leaf is pure, 35 levels deep with 118 leaves. Tree 2 peaks at depth 12 (0.802), and tree 3 levels off near 0.73 from depth 10. Tree 4 already reaches 0.80 with a single question about one word and stays at about 0.88 to 0.90 from depth 4. The Gini and entropy curves lie almost on top of each other for all four trees.


Accuracy and confusion matrices
Each confusion matrix has the true role family on its rows and the predicted one on its columns, so correct predictions lie on the diagonal. Tree 1, which uses every feature, is the most accurate. Its Gini tree labels 92.2% of test postings correctly, close to the best Naive Bayes model (93.5%), and finds 26 of the 33 forward_deployed postings (figure 2). Removing department drops accuracy to 76.7%, and only 12 of the 33 forward_deployed postings are found (figure 3). Removing company as well costs just another 1.3 points with Gini, to 75.4%, but the tree now finds only 10 of the 33 forward_deployed postings (figure 4). In trees 2 and 3, most mistakes on the two smaller classes go to software_eng, the largest class. Tree 4, which reads the masked description text, reaches 88.8% and finds 27 of the 33 forward_deployed postings, more than any other model on this page or the Naive Bayes page (figure 5). Overall it is still 2.6 points below Multinomial Naive Bayes and 4.7 below Bernoulli Naive Bayes on the same text, because it misses more of the solutions and software_eng postings.


The four trees
Figures 6 to 9 show the top two levels of each Gini tree. The full trees are 12 to 35 levels deep, so deeper nodes are cut off and shown as (…). Each box gives the question asked, the Gini impurity, the number of training postings that reach it, how many of them are in each class, and the majority class. The class counts in the diagrams follow scikit-learn’s alphabetical order, forward_deployed, software_eng and solutions, which is different from the order used everywhere else on this page. For example, the San Francisco box in tree 1 reads [14, 341, 17]: 14 forward_deployed, 341 software_eng and 17 solutions postings, the same group described below as 14, 17 and 341. A question such as “location_clean = San Francisco, CA <= 0.5” is true for postings outside San Francisco, so those go left.
All three trees built on posting facts start with the same question: is the job in San Francisco? Of the 372 San Francisco training postings, 341 are software_eng, so this one question picks out a large group that is almost all one class. In tree 1, every question shown below it is about department (figure 6). “Field Engineering - Other” alone picks out a group of 75 postings that are all solutions, and “Professional Services Operations” is asked on both sides. The tree is sorting postings by the employers’ own team names.
Without department, tree 2 turns to the employer instead (figure 7). Its next questions ask whether the company is Databricks, Palantir, Harvey or Asana. Databricks postings outside San Francisco form the only group in its top two levels where solutions is the majority, 146 of 271, because Databricks posts most of the solutions jobs in the data. Tree 3 has neither department nor company, so it asks about other locations, Bengaluru and New York, about the top of the salary range and about description length (figure 8). Every group in its top two levels still has software_eng as its majority, so forward_deployed and solutions are only separated further down, in small groups of postings. That fits its gap of 14.5 points between training and test accuracy.
Tree 4 reads the description text, and each of its questions is about the TF-IDF weight of one word (figure 9). Its first question is how much a posting uses the word “sales”. Of the 222 postings that use it most, 180 are solutions. Among the rest, the postings that use the word “travel” most are mostly forward_deployed, 79 of 102, so the need to travel is a strong sign of a forward deployed job in this tree.


What the trees rely on
Feature importance adds up how much each feature lowers the Gini impurity across all the splits in a tree, scaled so the total is 1. In tree 1, department accounts for 58.8% of the importance, almost three times as much as location (20.5%), while company adds 8.9% and description length 7.1% (figure 10). Salary contributes little, 3.2% from the bottom of the range and nothing from the top, partly because it is missing for 69% of postings. Without department, location (41.6%) and description length (28.3%) take over in tree 2, ahead of company (17.5%) (figure 11). In tree 3, location (44.9%) and description length (34.3%) together make up nearly four-fifths of the importance, with the bottom of the salary range a distant third at 9.1% (figure 12).


A split worked through
The root split of tree 1 repeats the calculation from the Overview on the real data. Before the split, the 927 training postings, 130 forward_deployed, 220 solutions and 577 software_eng, have a Gini impurity of 0.5366 and an entropy of 1.3157 bits. The San Francisco question sends 555 postings (116, 203 and 236) one way and 372 postings (14, 17 and 341) the other. The weighted Gini impurity of the two groups is 0.4469, a decrease of 0.0897, and their weighted entropy is 1.1137 bits, an information gain of 0.2019. The San Francisco group is far purer than the parent, at 92% software_eng. Lower down, the question about “Professional Services Operations” gives a smaller gain, 0.0808 for Gini and 0.1830 bits for entropy, but it picks out a group of 46 postings of which 43 are forward_deployed.


Why department works so well
Department is the team name each employer gives on its job board, copied unchanged for all 1,159 postings, and it is not taken from the job title. Yet 1,023 of the 1,159 postings (88.3%) sit in a department that is at least 90% one role family. Separately, 221 postings are in departments whose names contain a role phrase, such as “Field Engineering”, “Delivery Solutions Architects” or “Forward Deployed Engineering”. Every one of tree 1’s 232 test predictions passes through at least one question about department, and for 53.4% of them the last question before the answer is about department. Tree 1’s accuracy therefore largely reflects how closely each employer’s team names follow its job titles.
Leaving a column out does not fully remove what it carries. A tree using only tree 3’s features can name the employer of 71.6% of test postings, against 32.3% for always guessing Databricks, mainly from description length and location. Companies write to different lengths, from a median of 3,203 characters at Perplexity to 9,411 at Amplitude, and 90.7% of the Bengaluru postings are from Databricks. In the same way, tree 2’s features recover the department 44.4% of the time, against 15.5% for always guessing the most common one.

title: Decision Trees
text:
Conclusions
Facts about a job posting other than its description can sort these three kinds of technical work well, but mostly because employers already name their teams after the job. Using every available fact, about 92 in every 100 new postings were sorted correctly, compared with 62 from always guessing software engineering. Most of that came from the team name. Many employers place solutions engineers in teams with names like Field Engineering, and forward deployed engineers in a team called Forward Deployed Engineering, so the team name says almost as much as the job title.
Without the team name, much less can be told. Knowing the employer, where the job is, whether it is remote, what it pays when that is published, how long its description is and a few similar details, about 77 in every 100 postings were sorted correctly, and about 75 once the employer was left out as well. Forward deployed jobs become very hard to spot this way, and only about one in three was found. In location, pay and working arrangement, a forward deployed job looks much like any other engineering job.
The facts that remain still point to the employer. Where a job is and how long its description runs are enough to name the employer for about 7 in 10 postings, because each company writes at its own length and hires in its own places. Much of what these questions learn is how each company organises and describes its hiring, rather than what the jobs involve.
Reading the description itself works best for spotting forward deployed jobs. Questions about which words a posting uses found 27 of 33 forward deployed postings that had not been seen before, more than any other method tried on these pages, and two simple signals stood out: talking about sales points to a solutions job, and talking about travel points to a forward deployed one. This agrees with the previous page, where the description text alone told these jobs apart, and leads to one conclusion. What sets the forward deployed engineer apart is the work it describes, going out to customers and delivering results inside their business, not the team, place or pay attached to it. For the question of how AI is changing tech hiring, the new role shows up most clearly in what the job asks people to do.

title: Clustering
text:
Clustering is a way of finding groups in data without being told what the groups are. The method looks at how similar items are to each other and puts similar items together. No labels are given, so the groups come from the data alone. This makes clustering a tool for discovery. It can show patterns that nobody set out to look for.
There are two main kinds of clustering. Partitional clustering splits the data into a fixed number of groups, called k, which is chosen in advance. This project uses k-means. It places k centre points, assigns every item to its nearest centre, and then moves each centre to the middle of its group. It repeats this until the centres stop moving. Hierarchical clustering does not need k at the start. It begins with every item in a group of its own and keeps joining the two closest groups until only one group is left. The result is a tree, called a dendrogram, that can be cut at any height to give a set of groups.
Both methods need a way to measure how far apart two items are. Here the items are job postings, turned into word weights. The hierarchical clustering uses cosine similarity. It compares which words two postings use and how strongly, no matter how long each posting is. Groups are joined with complete linkage, which means two groups only count as close if even their least similar postings are close. K-means uses ordinary straight-line distance, called Euclidean distance. Every posting is scaled to the same size first, so this ranks pairs of postings in the same order as cosine similarity does.
In this project, clustering is run on 3,718 job postings from AI companies. The goal is to see which groups of jobs appear when the method reads only the job descriptions. Each posting already has a role family, such as software engineering, sales or forward deployed engineering, which was taken from its job title. That label is kept aside during clustering. It is only brought back afterwards, to check whether the groups the method found match the job types or something else.



The same 15 made-up points grouped in two ways. K-means splits them into a set number of groups around centre points. Hierarchical clustering builds a tree of merges, which can be cut at any height to give groups.





Postings A and B use words in the same mix, but B is longer. They are far apart in straight-line distance, yet the angle between them is 0, so cosine treats them as alike. Posting C is closer to A in straight-line distance but uses a different mix of words. This is why cosine suits text.

title: Clustering
text:
Data Preparation
Clustering works by measuring distances, and distances can only be measured between numbers. So the input has to be a table of numbers, with one row for each posting and one column for each feature. It also has to be unlabeled. If the role family were part of the input, the method would simply sort postings by the answer instead of finding groups on its own. For this reason the role family was removed before clustering and only used later to check the results.
The data started with 4,294 postings. Of these, 933 belonged to 357 groups of near copies, where a company posted the same job, with the same title and the same opening text, more than once. Only the first copy of each job was kept, and the other 576 copies were removed, so that repeated text could not form fake groups. That left 3,718 postings. Each description was then turned into numbers with a method called TF-IDF. Every posting becomes a row and every word becomes a column. A word gets a high weight in a posting when it is used often in that posting but is rare across all postings. Common English words such as “the” and “and” were dropped. So were words that appear in fewer than 5 postings or in more than 80% of them. This left about 7,800 word columns.
A first test showed a problem. Each company repeats the same blocks of text in all of its postings, such as its mission statement, its benefits and its legal notices. These blocks were so strong that the clusters grouped postings by company rather than by job. So a second version of the data was made. Any sentence that appears in at least 10% of one company’s postings, and in at least 3 of them, was removed, and so were company names. This cut the typical description roughly in half, from about 6,300 to about 3,300 characters, and left 7,495 word columns. Both versions were clustered, and both are shown in the results below.


Before: ten job postings as they arrive, each a company, a job title, a role family and a block of description text (only the first 120 characters are shown). Company boilerplate is then removed, the role family is set aside, and TF-IDF turns every posting into a row of word weights, shown in the next table.



After: the same ten postings and twelve of the 7,495 word columns from the version with company text removed. Each number is a TF-IDF weight. Many cells are zero, because each posting uses only a small share of all the words. There is no label column, only numbers.

title: Clustering
text:
Results
Clustering was run on two versions of the TF-IDF table: the raw descriptions, and the version with company boilerplate removed. For each version, k-means was fitted for every k from 2 to 15 with five random starts, and a complete-linkage tree was built on cosine distance. The numbers below refer to the figures further down the page.

Which values of k were compared
The silhouette score, inertia and stability across random starts were measured for every k from 2 to 15. Four values, k = 3, 4, 8 and 14, were then fitted and compared side by side, with their cluster sizes and silhouette plots (figures 2 and 6). These four include the k finally chosen for each version: k = 14 for the raw descriptions and k = 4 once boilerplate was removed.


What the silhouette score says about the best k
On the raw descriptions, the average silhouette score rises with k and is highest at k = 14 and k = 15, which tie at 0.173 (figure 1). Of every k close to that top, k = 14 also gives the most repeatable clusters across random starts, so it was chosen. Among the four values compared, the silhouette rises from 0.077 at k = 3 to 0.185 at k = 14.
Once company boilerplate is removed, the silhouette score is below 0.03 at every k (figure 5). It is highest at k = 15, the top of the range tested, so it does not point to a clear best k. Here k = 4 was chosen instead, as the largest k whose clusters stay the same across random starts. The low scores mean the groups overlap heavily: between 24% and 37% of postings sit closer to another cluster than to their own (figure 6).


Silhouette plots
Figures 2, 3, 6 and 7 show the silhouette value of every posting, grouped by cluster. On the raw descriptions (figure 3), only one cluster, a mix of smaller companies, has any postings with negative values. With boilerplate removed (figure 7), the sales and customer-facing technical clusters hold together, while the engineering cluster and the legal and finance cluster have many negative values.


How hierarchical clustering compares with k-means
On the raw descriptions the two methods agree fairly well, with an adjusted Rand index of 0.70 (figure 11). Both group postings by company: the hierarchical clusters H6 and H9 sit entirely inside the OpenAI and Databricks k-means clusters. The tree keeps the original distances well, with a cophenetic correlation of 0.85.
With boilerplate removed, agreement drops to 0.21 (figure 14). The tree splits the postings into two large groups, engineering (1,809 postings) and everything else (1,892), plus two tiny groups of 11 and 6 postings. K-means goes further and also separates sales, customer-facing technical work and a legal and finance group. The tree’s cophenetic correlation is 0.54, so it only roughly reflects the distances between postings.


What k the hierarchical tree suggests
The gaps between merge heights in the tree are all very small, so the dendrogram on its own does not mark a clear place to cut. Scoring every possible cut with the silhouette score gives a clearer answer. On the raw descriptions the best cut is k = 14 (figure 9), the same k chosen for k-means. With boilerplate removed, the silhouette of the cuts is almost flat. It is highest at k = 7, with the same value at k = 4 (figure 12), which matches the k chosen for k-means, while the k-means silhouette itself keeps rising up to k = 15.



  
    
  
  
    1. Choosing k for k-means (raw descriptions)
    Inertia has no clear elbow. The silhouette score is highest at k = 14 and k = 15, which tie at 0.173, and of every k within the seed-to-seed spread of that top, k = 14 is also the most stable across random starts (0.901), so it was chosen. The dip at k = 13 is a poor fit rather than real structure, since inertia rises there (2,285 to 2,292).
  



  
    
  
  
    2. Silhouette values at k = 3, 4, 8 and 14 (raw descriptions)
    The average silhouette rises from 0.077 at k = 3 to 0.185 at k = 14, and the share of postings with negative values falls to 2.9%, so k = 14 is the best of the four.
  



  
    
  
  
    3. Silhouette values for the chosen k = 14 (raw descriptions)
    Most postings fit their own cluster well: K1, a mix of smaller companies, is the only cluster with any negative values (36% of its postings, mean 0.01), while small single-company clusters such as Ramp (K4, 0.41) and Figma (K3, 0.38) score highest.
  



  
    
  
  
    4. Role family mix of each k-means cluster (raw descriptions)
    No cluster lines up with a role family: "other" is the largest group in 12 of the 14 clusters. Instead, the clusters follow employers, and 12 of them hold postings from a single company, because each company repeats the same boilerplate text in every posting.
  



  
    
  
  
    5. Choosing k for k-means (company boilerplate removed)
    Silhouette is below 0.03 at every k, so it cannot pick a k; k = 4 was chosen as the largest k whose clusters stay the same across random starts (agreement 0.88, falling to 0.75 at k = 5).
  



  
    
  
  
    6. Silhouette values at k = 3, 4, 8 and 14 (company boilerplate removed)
    Across the four k values compared, the average silhouette stays between 0.011 and 0.025, and 24% to 37% of postings have negative values, so none of them gives well-separated groups.
  



  
    
  
  
    7. Silhouette values for the chosen k = 4 (company boilerplate removed)
    The customer-technical (K1) and sales (K3) clusters hold together, while engineering (K2) and the legal and finance cluster (K0) are weak, with 34% and 69% of their postings negative.
  



  
    
  
  
    8. Role family mix of each k-means cluster (company boilerplate removed)
    With boilerplate removed, the clusters follow job types: K3 is 68% sales, K2 is 45% software engineering, and K1 is mainly solutions (43%) and forward_deployed (17%) postings.
  



  
    
  
  
    9. Which k the hierarchical tree suggests (raw descriptions)
    The merge gaps are all tiny, so the dendrogram itself does not point to one k, but the cut silhouette is highest at k = 14 (0.192), the same k chosen for k-means.
  



  
    
  
  
    10. Hierarchical clustering dendrogram (raw descriptions)
    The branches follow companies rather than jobs; for example, H9 is 716 Databricks postings and H6 is 694 OpenAI postings. The cophenetic correlation of 0.85 means the tree keeps the original distances well; average linkage scores higher (0.93) but was not used, because it puts 2,943 of the 3,718 postings into just two clusters.
  



  
    
  
  
    11. Hierarchical clusters against k-means clusters (raw descriptions)
    The two methods agree fairly well (ARI = 0.70). Two large hierarchical clusters sit entirely inside one k-means cluster each: H6 (694 postings) inside the OpenAI cluster K8, and H9 (716) inside the Databricks cluster K7. Others are merged, with H3 combining Anthropic (517), Scale AI (199) and Cohere (134).
  



  
    
  
  
    12. Which k the hierarchical tree suggests (company boilerplate removed)
    The cut silhouette is almost flat, with its highest value at k = 7 and an equal value at k = 4 (both 0.025), which matches the k chosen for k-means; the k-means silhouette is instead highest at k = 15, the top of the range tested.
  



  
    
  
  
    13. Hierarchical clustering dendrogram (company boilerplate removed)
    The tree really splits postings into two groups: H1 (1,809 postings) is the engineering group, H0 (1,892) mixes sales, solutions and forward_deployed postings, and the other two clusters are tiny (11 and 6 postings).
  



  
    
  
  
    14. Hierarchical clusters against k-means clusters (company boilerplate removed)
    Agreement is low (ARI = 0.21): hierarchical clustering mainly separates engineering (H1 holds 1,247 of 1,496 K2 postings) from everything else, while k-means also splits out sales, customer-technical and legal/finance groups.

title: Clustering
text:
Conclusions
The clearest lesson is that job postings at AI companies are written mostly in the company’s own voice. On the raw descriptions, 12 of the 14 clusters each hold postings from a single employer, and the clusters match the company far more closely than the type of job. Mission statements, benefits and legal notices are repeated in every posting and drown out the description of the work itself. Any study of hiring that reads posting text has to remove this boilerplate first, or it will measure employers instead of jobs.
Once the boilerplate is removed, the descriptions do sort into kinds of work: engineering, sales, customer-facing technical work, and a broad business group covering roles such as legal, finance and operations. These groups match the role families much better than before, but they still overlap a great deal. About a third of postings sit closer to another group than to their own. Jobs at these companies blend into each other more than their titles suggest.
This matters most for forward deployed engineers. Their descriptions do not form a group of their own. The customer-facing technical cluster holds 78% of solutions postings and 52% of forward deployed postings, while another 42% of forward deployed postings fall in the engineering cluster. In the words companies use, the role sits between solutions work and engineering, and closer to solutions than its “engineer” title suggests. Customer-facing technical work as a whole does stand out as a group of its own, with 493 of the 3,718 postings.
Finally, the two methods only agree fairly closely on the raw text, where the company signal is easy to find. On the cleaned text, the hierarchical tree mainly separates engineering from everything else, while k-means also splits out sales and customer-facing work. The split between engineering and non-engineering jobs is the one result that both methods support.

title: Naive Bayes
text:
Naive Bayes is a supervised method for classification. It learns from examples whose class is already known and then predicts the class of new examples. It is built on Bayes’ theorem, which turns the question “how likely is this class, given these features?” around into “how likely are these features, given this class?”. The second question can be answered by counting in the training data. For each class, the method takes the class’s share of the training data, called the prior, multiplies it by the probability of each feature within that class, and picks the class with the highest result.
The word “naive” refers to one simplifying assumption: within a class, every feature is treated as independent of every other. For text, this means each word is scored on its own, as if the words in a document had nothing to do with each other. That is clearly not true, but the method still works well in practice, because it only has to rank the classes in the right order, not get every probability exactly right. It is fast, needs little training data and copes with thousands of features. This is why it is widely used for spam filtering, sorting news articles or support tickets by topic, judging whether reviews are positive or negative, and as a quick first model that other models can be compared against.
Two practical details matter. Multiplying many small probabilities gives numbers too small for a computer to store, so the logarithms of the probabilities are added up instead, which picks the same winner. And a word that never appears in a class’s training documents would get a probability of zero, which would rule that class out no matter what else the document says. Smoothing fixes this by adding a small amount, called alpha, to every word count before the probabilities are worked out. With alpha = 1 this is known as Laplace smoothing, and smaller values change the counts less.
There are several kinds of Naive Bayes, which differ in how they describe each document. Multinomial Naive Bayes, the standard version for text, works with how often each word appears, so a word used three times in a document counts three times. It is usually given word counts, but it also accepts weighted counts such as TF-IDF. Bernoulli Naive Bayes describes each document only by which words it contains, as a list of yes-or-no values, so a word used once and a word used ten times count the same. Unlike the multinomial version, it also uses the words that are missing. For every word in the vocabulary that a document does not contain, it multiplies in the chance that a document of that class leaves the word out. This makes Bernoulli Naive Bayes suited to short texts and to any data made of yes-or-no features. A third kind, Gaussian Naive Bayes, is used for continuous measurements such as heights or prices.
This project uses Naive Bayes to ask whether the text of a job posting can tell three closely related technical jobs apart: forward deployed engineering, solutions roles such as solutions engineer and solutions architect, and software engineering. The Introduction describes the forward deployed engineer as one of the fastest-growing jobs at AI companies, a role that mixes engineering with working alongside customers. If the descriptions of these jobs can be told apart, they are different kinds of work. If the model keeps mixing them up, the new role overlaps with the older ones. Both the multinomial and the Bernoulli versions are fitted and compared.



The same made-up document read by the two kinds of Naive Bayes. Multinomial Naive Bayes counts how often each word appears, so “data”, used three times, brings in its probability three times, and words that do not appear drop out. Bernoulli Naive Bayes only asks whether each word appears, so “data” counts once, and every vocabulary word that is missing also counts as evidence, through the chance that the class leaves it out.





Naive Bayes scoring the three-word document “goal match vote” for two made-up classes. Each class starts from its prior and adds the log probability of each word, and the higher total wins: class A, with −6.02 against −6.70. The word “vote” never appears in class A’s training words, so without smoothing its probability is zero and class A could never win, and the document would go to class B. Adding 1 to every count (alpha = 1) gives “vote” a small probability and changes the answer.

For every word in the vocabulary that a document does not contain, it multiplies in the chance that a document of that class leaves the word out. This makes Bernoulli Naive Bayes suited to short texts and to any data made of yes-or-no features. A third kind, Gaussian Naive Bayes, is used for continuous measurements such as heights or prices.
This project uses Naive Bayes to ask whether the text of a job posting can tell three closely related technical jobs apart: forward deployed engineering, solutions roles such as solutions engineer and solutions architect, and software engineering. The Introduction describes the forward deployed engineer as one of the fastest-growing jobs at AI companies, a role that mixes engineering with working alongside customers. If the descriptions of these jobs can be told apart, they are different kinds of work. If the model keeps mixing them up, the new role overlaps with the older ones. Both the multinomial and the Bernoulli versions are fitted and compared.



The same made-up document read by the two kinds of Naive Bayes. Multinomial Naive Bayes counts how often each word appears, so “data”, used three times, brings in its probability three times, and words that do not appear drop out. Bernoulli Naive Bayes only asks whether each word appears, so “data” counts once, and every vocabulary word that is missing also counts as evidence, through the chance that the class leaves it out.





Naive Bayes scoring the three-word document “goal match vote” for two made-up classes. Each class starts from its prior and adds the log probability of each word, and the higher total wins: class A, with −6.02 against −6.70. The word “vote” never appears in class A’s training words, so without smoothing its probability is zero and class A could never win, and the document would go to class B. Adding 1 to every count (alpha = 1) gives “vote” a small probability and changes the answer.

title: Naive Bayes
text:
Data Preparation
Naive Bayes is a supervised method, so it can only learn from labelled data. Every row needs the right answer attached, which here is the posting’s role family. The model learns which words go with which label, and a row without a label gives it nothing to learn from and nothing to check its predictions against. Only postings with a known role family can therefore be used. The role family was given to each posting earlier in the project from its job title, using keyword rules that are checked in order, with the first match deciding. A title containing “forward deployed” or “FDE” is labelled forward_deployed. A title containing “solutions engineer”, “solutions architect”, “solutions consultant”, “delivery”, “deployment strategist” or “technical account” is labelled solutions. A title containing “software engineer”, “backend”, “frontend”, “infrastructure”, “platform engineer” or “SRE” is labelled software_eng. The model never sees the title. It only reads the job description, so it has to work out the role from how the work is described.
The data starts from the same 4,294 cleaned job postings used on the Clustering page. As there, repeated copies of the same job were removed, leaving 3,718 postings. Only the three role families compared here were kept, which gives 1,159 postings: 721 software_eng, 275 solutions and 163 forward_deployed. The classes are uneven, and software_eng alone makes up 62% of the data.
Each description was prepared in three versions. The first is the raw text. The second removes company boilerplate with the same rule as the Clustering page: any sentence that appears in at least 10% of one company’s postings, and in at least 3 of them, is dropped, along with company names. This roughly halves the typical description, from about 5,950 to about 3,150 characters. The list of boilerplate sentences was found across all 3,718 postings, as on the Clustering page, so it also saw the postings later used for testing. Only the choice of which sentences to remove was made this way, and everything the models learn comes from the training set. The third version also masks the role. Because the labels come from job titles, and many descriptions repeat their title, a model could score well just by finding the title in the text. To prevent this, the posting’s own title and 24 role phrases, such as “forward deployed”, “FDE”, “solutions architect”, “software engineer” and the abbreviations “SA” and “DSA”, were removed. This changed 865 of the 1,159 descriptions but took out only a few words from each, a median of 38 characters.
The 1,159 postings were then split at random into a training set of 927 postings (80%) and a test set of 232 postings (20%). The model learns from the training set only. The test set is kept aside and used once, at the end, to measure how well the model labels postings it has never seen. The split was stratified, so each role family has the same share in both sets: 130 forward_deployed, 220 solutions and 577 software_eng postings in training, and 33, 55 and 144 in testing. The two sets are disjoint, meaning no posting is in both, and this was checked by job ID. This matters because a model tested on postings it was trained on is being asked questions it has already seen the answers to, so its score would overstate how well it works on new data. The same split is used for every model on this page.
Finally, the text has to become numbers. Naive Bayes in scikit-learn, the Python library used here, only accepts numeric input, so each description is turned into one row of numbers with one column per word. For Multinomial Naive Bayes the numbers are TF-IDF weights, as on the Clustering page: a word scores high in a posting when it is used often there but is rare across postings. For Bernoulli Naive Bayes each number is 1 if the word appears in the posting and 0 if it does not. Common English words were dropped, and so were words found in fewer than 5 training postings or in more than 80% of them. Every word also has to contain at least one letter, so bare numbers are ignored. In this data the numbers that stood out most were salary bands, mostly from one company, such as $182,000 to $250,208, and these say who is hiring rather than what the job is. The vocabulary was learned from the training set alone and then applied to the test set, so words that appear only in test postings are ignored. On the masked text this gives 3,631 word columns.


Labelled input: ten of the 1,159 postings, each with its role family label and the first 120 characters of its masked description. Company names and role phrases have been taken out, which leaves gaps such as “As a on the Product Engineering team at ,”. The label is what the model learns to predict, and the description is the only thing it reads.



Training set: ten of the 927 training postings, after the masked text has been turned into TF-IDF weights. Only eight of the 3,631 word columns are shown, the eight words found in the most training postings. A weight of 0 means the posting does not use that word. The label stays next to the numbers, because the model learns from both.



Test set: ten of the 232 test postings, turned into numbers with the vocabulary learned from the training set. No job ID appears in both sets. The model only sees the word columns here, and the labels are used afterwards to check its predictions.

Macro F1 averages the F1 score of the three classes, so the small forward_deployed class counts as much as the large software_eng class. It is lower than accuracy for every model because the smaller classes are harder to get right.

Accuracy
On the raw descriptions, Multinomial Naive Bayes labels 83.6% of test postings correctly and Bernoulli Naive Bayes 73.7% (figure 1). Removing company boilerplate lifts them to 91.8% and 93.5%. The raw text is dominated by sentences that each company repeats in its postings, such as its mission statement and its benefits, and these say who is hiring rather than what the job is. Bernoulli Naive Bayes suffers most. One likely reason is that it only records whether a word appears, so the hundreds of boilerplate words in a posting count as much as the few words about the work. Masking the role phrases then makes almost no difference: Multinomial Naive Bayes drops by one posting to 91.4%, and Bernoulli Naive Bayes makes exactly the same predictions as before. The best model, Bernoulli Naive Bayes on the masked text, labels 217 of the 232 test postings correctly.


Confusion matrices
The confusion matrices in figures 2 to 4 show where the mistakes fall. Each row is the true role family and each column the predicted one, so correct predictions lie on the diagonal. On the masked text, Bernoulli Naive Bayes finds 143 of the 144 software_eng postings, 49 of the 55 solutions postings and 25 of the 33 forward_deployed postings (figure 4). Forward_deployed is the hardest class, and its misses are split between solutions (5) and software_eng (3). The mistakes mostly run in one direction, though. Only one posting from another class is wrongly called forward_deployed, so when the model predicts forward_deployed it is right 25 times out of 26.


Whether the models were reading the job title
Before masking, the title rule finds “forward deployed” or “FDE” in the description itself for 130 of the 163 forward_deployed postings. After masking, it finds them in just 1. Even so, Bernoulli Naive Bayes recognises 25 of the 33 forward_deployed test postings on the masked text, the same number as before masking. Figure 5 shows the words each class uses most. The lists overlap a lot: data, ai, product and engineering are in the top 15 for all three families, so on their own these words say little about which job a posting is for. title: Naive Bayes
text:
Conclusions
The way a job is described is enough to tell these three kinds of technical work apart most of the time. After learning from four out of every five postings, the method correctly sorted about 93 in every 100 of the postings it had not seen, compared with 62 in every 100 from simply guessing software engineering every time. This still held after job titles and role names were taken out of the text, so the difference comes from the work each posting describes, not from what the job is called.
The three jobs are described in clearly different words. Software engineering postings talk about building and running large systems. Solutions postings talk about selling and showing the product, through demos, workshops and trial projects for prospective customers. Forward deployed postings talk about results delivered inside a client’s business: working embedded with the client, on high-stakes priorities, with outcomes that can be measured. Put simply, one job builds the product, one sells it, and one puts it to work at the customer.
Forward deployed engineering is the hardest of the three to recognise. Between a quarter and a third of forward deployed postings were mistaken for one of the other two jobs, split between solutions roles and software engineering. Yet when a posting was identified as forward deployed, that was almost always correct. The role has a voice of its own, but it shares much of its language with customer-facing technical sales. This matches the Clustering page, where forward deployed postings sat between solutions work and engineering, and closer to solutions.
Two further lessons carry over to the wider topic. First, the standard text that companies repeat in their postings once again hides the job. When each company’s text about its mission and benefits was left in, the method made two to four times as many mistakes. Second, employers use the forward deployed title for a wide range of jobs, from security engineers to program and partner managers, which is part of why the role is harder to pin down. For the question of how AI is changing tech hiring, the forward deployed engineer looks like a genuinely new kind of job rather than a new name for software engineering, but one that draws on the language of customer-facing sales as much as on engineering.

title: Regression
text:
Linear regression is a supervised method that predicts a number. It assumes that the number to be predicted, called the target, is a weighted sum of the features plus a constant: predicted value = b0 + b1·x1 + b2·x2 + …. Each weight, or coefficient, says how much the prediction changes when its feature goes up by one unit while every other feature stays the same. The weights are chosen by least squares, which picks the line, or in more dimensions the flat surface, that makes the sum of the squared differences between the predicted and the actual values as small as possible. Linear regression is quick to fit and easy to read, and it is used for tasks such as forecasting sales, estimating house prices from size and location, and studying how pay depends on experience and occupation.
Logistic regression is also a supervised method, but it predicts a class rather than a number. In its basic form it answers a yes-or-no question, such as whether an email is spam, whether a patient has a disease or whether a customer will leave, and it gives the probability that the answer is yes. It starts from the same kind of weighted sum as linear regression, called the linear score, z = b0 + b1·x1 + b2·x2 + …, but it does not use the score itself as the prediction. That matters because a probability has to stay between 0 and 1, while a straight line keeps rising or falling without limit. A straight line fitted to a 0/1 outcome predicts values below 0 and above 1, which are not probabilities (first figure below).
Logistic regression passes the linear score through the sigmoid function, p = 1 / (1 + exp(−z)), which turns any score into a probability between 0 and 1 (second figure below). A score of 0 gives exactly 0.5, large positive scores give probabilities close to 1, and large negative scores give probabilities close to 0. For example, a score of 1 gives 1 / (1 + exp(−1)) = 0.731, and a score of −2 gives 1 / (1 + exp(2)) = 0.119. The probability becomes a class by comparing it with a threshold. With the usual threshold of 0.5, the model predicts yes when p is at least 0.5, which is the same as a linear score of at least 0. Moving the threshold trades one kind of mistake for another. A lower threshold finds more of the true yes cases, which raises recall, but it also lets in more false alarms, which lowers precision. A higher threshold does the reverse.
The coefficients of a logistic regression are read through the odds, the probability of yes divided by the probability of no. The linear score is the logarithm of the odds, so raising a feature by one unit adds its coefficient to the log odds and multiplies the odds by exp(coefficient), a number called the odds ratio. An odds ratio above 1 makes yes more likely and one below 1 makes it less likely. The coefficients are found by maximum likelihood, which picks the values that make the labels in the training data most probable, usually with a penalty that keeps the coefficients from growing too large. In scikit-learn, the Python library used here, the strength of that penalty is set by C: a smaller C means a stronger penalty and smaller coefficients.
The two methods therefore differ in what they predict and in how they are judged. Linear regression predicts a number and is judged by how far its predictions fall from the true values, for example with the root mean squared error (RMSE), the mean absolute error (MAE) and R², the share of the variation in the target that the model explains. Logistic regression predicts a probability and a class, and it is judged like any classifier, with a confusion matrix, accuracy, precision and recall.
This project uses both. Linear regression predicts the salary a job posting advertises, the midpoint of its pay range, from facts about the posting: its company, department, location, working arrangement, role family and the length of its description. The question is how much of the pay on offer depends on the kind of job and how much on the employer. Logistic regression asks a yes-or-no version of the question from the Naive Bayes page: is a posting a forward deployed engineering job or not, judged only from the words of its description? Its results are compared with Naive Bayes models fitted to the same question.



The same made-up input, hours studied, predicting two kinds of target. Left: linear regression predicts an exam score, a number, with the line score = 47.91 + 4.21 × hours, which predicts 107 points at 14 hours. Right: a straight line fitted to pass (1) or fail (0) runs from −0.14 at 0 hours to 1.23 at 14 hours, outside the range of a probability, while the logistic curve stays between 0 and 1 and crosses 0.5 at 6.5 hours.





The sigmoid and the threshold, with made-up numbers. Left: the sigmoid turns a linear score z into a probability p. A score of −2 gives 0.119, a score of 0 gives 0.5 and a score of 1 gives 0.731, and at the usual threshold of 0.5 every score above 0 is predicted yes. Right: for 12 made-up yes cases and 12 no cases, raising the threshold from 0.3 to 0.7 raises precision from 0.65 to 0.83 but lowers recall from 0.92 to 0.42.
